Urban Green Spaces and Healthy Cities

Parks, gardens and tree-lined streets are among the most valuable features of a city. They offer places to rest and play, support wildlife, cool the air and help manage rainwater. As cities grow denser, planners are paying closer attention to how green spaces are designed, distributed and maintained.

Parks and public health

Regular access to green space is linked to better physical and mental health. People who live near parks tend to walk more, and children who play outdoors develop stronger motor skills. Time spent among trees and plants is associated with lower stress and improved mood. Parks also give neighbours a place to meet, which can strengthen community ties and reduce loneliness.

The benefits depend on more than the size of a park. Safe paths, good lighting, seating, toilets and drinking water all affect how often people visit. A small, well-maintained pocket park within a short walk of home can be used more often than a large park that requires a long journey.

Biodiversity in the city

Cities can support a surprising variety of plants and animals. Native trees and shrubs provide food and shelter for birds and insects. Meadows that are mown only once or twice a year allow wildflowers to bloom and pollinators to thrive. Ponds and wetlands attract amphibians and dragonflies. Connecting green spaces with corridors of trees and hedges allows species to move between them.

Residents can help by planting native species in gardens and on balconies, leaving some areas untidy for insects, and avoiding pesticides. Schools and community groups often take part in surveys that help scientists understand how urban wildlife is changing.

Stormwater management

Hard surfaces such as roads and roofs prevent rain from soaking into the ground. During heavy storms, water runs off quickly, overloading drains and causing floods. Green infrastructure slows this flow. Rain gardens, planted swales and permeable paving allow water to soak in, while green roofs hold rain and release it slowly. Trees intercept rainfall on their leaves and draw water from the soil.

These features also filter pollutants from runoff before it reaches rivers and lakes. Many cities now require new developments to manage a share of their rainwater on site, which encourages designs that include planting rather than relying only on pipes.

Accessibility and fairness

Green space is not always shared equally. Wealthier neighbourhoods often have more trees and larger parks, while poorer areas may have few. Planners increasingly measure how far each household lives from a usable green space and prioritise improvements where access is lowest. Paths should be wide and level enough for wheelchairs and prams, and signs should be clear and available in the languages spoken locally.

Involving residents in design helps ensure that parks meet real needs. Older people may want shaded seating and gentle walking routes, teenagers may want sports courts and places to gather, and families may want play areas and picnic spots.

Community gardens

Community gardens allow people without private land to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. They provide fresh food, teach practical skills and bring together people of different ages and backgrounds. Many gardens host workshops on composting, seed saving and cooking. Some work with schools, hospitals or food banks.

Successful gardens usually have clear rules for sharing plots and tools, reliable access to water, and a small group of volunteers who coordinate activities. Support from the local council, such as secure land tenure, can make the difference between a garden that lasts for decades and one that disappears after a few seasons.

Climate resilience

Green spaces help cities cope with a changing climate. Trees shade streets and buildings, lowering temperatures during heatwaves. Vegetation absorbs carbon dioxide, and healthy soils store carbon. Wetlands and floodplains provide room for water during extreme rainfall. Planting a mix of species makes urban greenery more resistant to pests, diseases and drought.

Investing in green infrastructure is often cheaper than building and maintaining equivalent grey infrastructure, and it delivers many benefits at once. A city that values its parks, trees and gardens is better prepared for the challenges ahead and a more pleasant place to live.
